# Cohorts {#sec-cohorts}

This page defines the **full NCC cohort** and the **subcohorts** within it: who
counts as a participant, how the subcohorts are constituted, and how to select
one correctly in an analysis. For how participants are recruited and how their
data is gathered, see @sec-data-collection; for how the delivered datasets are
structured and joined, see
[Data management](../best-practices/data-management.qmd).

## The full cohort

The full NCC cohort is every participant who has consented to take part and has
not withdrawn. In the delivered data, that is every `deltaker_id` present in
the research-tier files for a given release.

Two properties follow from how the data is processed, and both matter when you
report a cohort size:

- **The cohort is defined by consent, not by response.** A participant is in
  the cohort once consent is recorded, whether or not they have answered any
  particular questionnaire. Someone who consented and then never completed a
  follow-up is still a cohort member with missing follow-up data — not a
  non-member.
- **The cohort is dynamic, not fixed.** Withdrawn consents are re-applied on
  *every* processing run, so a participant who withdraws is removed from all
  subsequently delivered datasets. Two releases of the same dataset can
  therefore have different row counts, and the difference is not an error.

::: {.callout-important}
Because the cohort changes between releases, a bare participant count is not
reproducible. Always state **which data release** a number refers to when you
report a cohort or subcohort size.
:::

## Kinds of subcohort

"Subcohort" is used loosely in day-to-day conversation for three quite
different things. They behave differently, and conflating them causes real
errors, so this page keeps them separate.

| Kind | Defined by | Membership is |
|------|-----------|---------------|
| **Recruited sub-study** | Enrolment into a distinct sub-study, usually with its own questionnaires and approvals | A fact about the participant, fixed at recruitment |
| **Response-defined group** | Which questionnaires a participant actually completed | A consequence of participation, changing as data accrues |
| **Analytic subgroup** | A variable value (e.g. infection status, vaccination status) | A choice made by the analyst, in code |

The distinction that matters most is between the first and the last. A
**recruited sub-study** has its own governance — its own aim, its own inclusion
criteria, possibly its own approvals — and you cannot construct or redefine it
yourself. An **analytic subgroup** is something you define in your analysis
script, and it is only as reproducible as the code that defines it.

::: {.callout-warning}
Do not describe an analytic subgroup as a sub-study in a manuscript. "The
long-COVID subcohort" means something different depending on whether
participants were *recruited* into it or *classified* into it after the fact,
and readers will assume the former.
:::

  the `R1_`–`R6_` prefixes.
- It is delivered as its own topic dataset, `cloc_dataset`.

## Topic datasets are not subcohorts

The delivered **topic datasets** — `cloc_dataset`, `long_covid_dataset`,
`vaccine_dataset` — are named after research areas, which makes it tempting to
read them as subcohort extracts. They are a *variable* selection: each one
bundles the forms, registry data, and derived variables relevant to a topic.

::: {.callout-warning}
Do not assume that a row in `cloc_dataset` means the participant is a CLOC
participant, or that the file's row count is the CLOC subcohort size.

A dataset scoped to a topic may still contain the whole cohort, with
non-members carrying missing values for the topic's variables — which is
exactly what a full join produces. Establish membership from a documented
membership rule, not from the file you happen to have loaded.
:::

## Selecting a subcohort in analysis

Once the membership rules are documented, apply them explicitly:

1. **Define membership in code, from a documented variable or rule.** Never
   define it by which file you loaded, and never by which rows happen to be
   non-missing.
2. **Filter on value codes, not label text.** Codes are stable across releases;
   label wording may be refined.
3. **Choose the join deliberately.** A full join keeps the whole cohort and
   represents non-membership as missing; an inner join silently drops everyone
   who is not in both files. For a subcohort analysis, an inner join is often
   what you want — but it should be a decision you made, not a side effect.
4. **Report the resulting size, and check it.** Assert the expected count
   rather than eyeballing it, so a changed release fails loudly instead of
   quietly shifting your denominator.

```r
library(tidyverse)

# Membership from a documented rule — not from which file was loaded.
# PLACEHOLDER: `membership_variable` and its code are not yet documented.
# Substitute the real variable and value code once the study team has
# recorded them above; filter on the code, never on the label text.
cloc_cohort <- full_dataset |>
  dplyr::filter(membership_variable == 1)

# Fail loudly if the release changed the size out from under the analysis.
stopifnot(
  nrow(cloc_cohort) == dplyr::n_distinct(cloc_cohort$deltaker_id)
)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Record the **data release** and the **membership rule** at the top of every
analysis script. Between them they make a participant count reproducible; a
count without them cannot be checked by anyone else.
:::

## Reporting cohorts in publications

Observational work from the study follows **STROBE** (and **RECORD** for the
registry-linked analyses), both of which expect the study population to be
described precisely.

For each analysis, state:

- the **data release** the numbers come from;
- how the **analysis population** was derived from the full cohort — the
  eligibility rule, the subcohort rule, and each exclusion applied;
- the **number excluded at each step**, so a participant flow diagram can be
  reconstructed;
- whether a subcohort was **recruited** or **defined analytically**.
